analysis.one_liner: Diverts surplus coal-mining reclamation funds to shore up retired coal miners' pensions.
analysis.headline: The Miners Pension Protection Act was introduced with 27 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a committee or floor vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Treasury Department, whenever annual coal-mining reclamation collections exceeded a $490 million limit, to send the surplus to the United Mine Workers' 1974 pension plan, which had fallen behind on its promises to retired miners and their widows. It required the pension fund to file detailed annual reports on its funding status as a safeguard. To offset the federal cost, it extended customs fees charged on imported goods by about four months.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired union coal miners, their surviving spouses, and pensioners in the 1974 United Mine Workers of America Pension Plan, whose benefits were at risk because the plan no longer had enough active workers paying in to cover its promised payouts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired union coal miners and widows

how_it_helps.text: Whenever annual transfers under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act's $490 million limit exceed what is owed for other purposes, including miners' health plans, the surplus must be sent to the 1974 UMWA Pension Plan to pay promised pension benefits [S2][S3].

The transfers continue until the plan's funded percentage reaches 100 percent, and the bill adds detailed annual reporting on the plan's funded status, cash flow, and employer withdrawals to Treasury and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation [S3].
The cost is offset by extending the collection of customs merchandise processing fees on imported goods from January 14, 2026 to May 13, 2026 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and importers bear modest costs: customs user fees on imported goods would be collected for about four additional months, and surplus abandoned-mine reclamation money would go to pensions instead of other reclamation uses.

drawbacks.text: The bill routes money from the abandoned mine reclamation fund away from other uses, relying on whatever surplus exists above the $490 million annual limit, which may not be enough in a given year to cover the plan's shortfall [S2][S3].

It does not change the underlying cause of the plan's underfunding: employers that withdrew from the plan and the shrinking number of active miners paying in, so transfers could continue indefinitely and the federal government effectively backstops a private pension [S3].
Extending the customs merchandise processing fee is a user charge on importers that can be passed to consumers in the price of imported goods [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core purpose is narrow and concrete: keeping pension checks flowing to retired miners and widows whose plan was underfunded through no fault of their own. The costs are modest and offset, and the bill adds real oversight reporting. The main honest criticism is design: it patches the pension with reclamation surplus year by year rather than fixing the funding structure, so the fix depends on collections holding up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and sent to an Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee two weeks later, but no committee ever voted it out and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley introduced the Miners Pension Protection Act in the House on May 25, 2017 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the Natural Resources Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
On June 14, 2017 it was referred to the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
It drew 27 cosponsors, 11 Republicans and 16 Democrats, but no further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, retired miners and widows got no new pension funding and remained exposed to benefit cuts, while importers paid no extended customs fees and no reclamation funds were redirected. Companies that had walked away from the plan kept paying nothing toward the shortfall.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retired miners left exposed; importers and withdrawing employers spared costs

for.name: Rep. David B. McKinley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 Republican and 16 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 27 House cosponsors
for.role: Cross-party group of 11 Republicans and 16 Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from coal and industrial states.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 25, 2017 and sent it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on June 14, 2017; never reported the bill out.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of sequential referral (jurisdiction over the customs-fee offset)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 25, 2017 and took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start, 11 Republicans and 16 Democrats among 27 cosponsors, and no recorded vote or recorded opposition ever occurred.

industries.industry: Retired union coal miners and UMWA pension beneficiaries
industries.note: These are the people the bill would have helped: tens of thousands of retired miners and widows drawing from an underfunded plan. With the bill dead, their benefits remained exposed to cuts.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies, including employers that withdrew from the 1974 UMWA plan
industries.note: Shoring up the plan with federal money keeps pension promises alive without requiring employers that created or abandoned the plan to pay more. The bill's reporting requirements list withdrawing employers and their withdrawal liability, an acknowledgment of that dynamic.
Importers would have paid merchandise processing fees about four months longer, through May 13, 2026, as the offset; those fees are typically passed into consumer prices.

industries.industry: Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation and federal pension oversight
industries.note: The bill would have given Treasury and the PBGC detailed annual reporting on the plan's funded status, giving regulators better information on a struggling multiemployer pension.
